On Saturday mornings, the library basement fills with objects that have stopped doing what they were made to do. Lamps arrive with dark bulbs and loose switches. Toasters arrive carrying the faint smell of their last successful breakfast. A woman once brought a music box in a shoebox padded with towels, as carefully as if she were transporting a bird. Above us, people return novels and argue quietly with the printer. Down here, among folding tables and extension cords, we try to persuade things to work again.

Our repair group began when Mara, who knows more about sewing machines than anyone I have met, put up a handwritten sign: **BROKEN? BRING IT BY.** She expected a few neighbors. Twelve people came the first week, some carrying appliances, others carrying tools, and several just curious. Four years later, we still meet twice a month. Nobody is in charge, though Mara knows where everything is and can make the room fall silent by asking who took her small screwdriver.

I came because of a radio. It was a squat brown one with a cracked dial, inherited from my grandfather. As a child, I had watched him tune it at the kitchen table, easing the needle through a storm of static until a voice emerged. He listened to baseball games, weather reports, and late-night conversations with strangers. After he died, the radio sat on my shelf. One winter, I plugged it in and got nothing—not even the soft pop it used to make when it woke up.

I carried it to the library in a grocery bag. Mara looked at the cloth-covered cord and told me, kindly but firmly, not to plug it in again. She introduced me to Dev, a retired electrician who had brought his own meter and a sandwich wrapped in wax paper. He showed me how to remove the back without breaking the brittle case. Inside was a miniature city of wires and dusty components. I had expected a single loose connection, something we could find and fix before lunch. Instead, Dev taught me how to look.

That is most of what happens in the basement. People come in hoping for a quick answer, and someone invites them to hold a flashlight or turn a screw. The work slows down. We ask when an object last worked and whether anything unusual happened before it failed. We look for scorch marks, frayed cords, worn teeth, and the tiny springs that leap out when a casing opens. We take photographs so we can remember how the pieces fit together. Sometimes the answer is simple. Often we have to admit that we do not know yet.

The radio took three Saturdays. A damaged cord was easy to identify, but replacing it did not bring back the sound. Dev and I tested one component after another while other repairs rose and fell around us. A child learned to patch a bicycle tube. Mara freed a jammed sewing machine and then spent an hour helping its owner thread it. Someone brought in a kettle with a handle too broken to make it safe to carry hot water. We could not repair that one. Its owner stayed anyway and helped sweep the floor.

On the third Saturday, Dev found a failed capacitor. He had suspected it earlier but wanted to show me how to rule out other faults. We replaced it, set the radio on the table, and kept our hands clear while he switched it on. The speaker crackled. Then came a burst of music, loud enough to make everyone turn. Dev grinned, though he had been warning me all morning that the repair might not work. We listened for a minute, and then I turned the dial slowly, searching through static the way my grandfather had.

I used to think a repair was valuable only if the object lasted afterward. By that measure, some mornings in the basement are failures. We cannot get parts for everything. Some devices are sealed so tightly that opening them does more damage. Once, after two hours of work, a blender ran for six seconds and stopped again. Its owner laughed, then looked disappointed, then helped us pack away the tools. I remembered his face later when I was deciding whether to throw out a lamp at home. I brought it in instead.

There is an economy to this work, though it rarely saves anyone much money. A new lamp can cost less than the time spent repairing an old one. What people save is harder to put on a receipt: the trouble of throwing something away, the worry that they should have known how to fix it, the distance between wanting to try and knowing where to begin. When a person leaves carrying an object that works, they usually carry a little more knowledge as well. When they leave without a repair, at least they know what went wrong.

I keep coming back for the workbench more than for the finished objects. At home, I can put a broken thing aside and forget it. In the basement, someone will ask what I have tried. Someone else will remember a similar problem. We disagree, borrow each other’s tools, lose screws, find them under chair legs, and make room for whoever walks in next. The room has taught me practical skills, but it has also made me less embarrassed to be a beginner. There are plenty of beginners there, including people who have been fixing things for decades.

My grandfather’s radio now lives in my kitchen. I turn it on while I make breakfast, though I still have to be careful with the dial; a slight movement can send the station drifting away. Some mornings I listen to the news. Some mornings I leave it between stations and hear only static while the kettle heats. I know that one day the radio may fail again. If it does, I will carry it back to the library, find an empty space at the table, and take off the back.
